A benchmark score is the output of a measurement system applied to one checkpoint. The system includes the task population, dataset version, prompt, tools, inference budget, answer parser, grader, aggregation rule, and uncertainty. Changing one component creates a different experiment.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture, you should be able to:

1. distinguish intrinsic, extrinsic, capability, preference, safety, and efficiency evaluation;
2. construct a reproducible scenario from checkpoint through aggregation;
3. choose exact match, pass@$k$, pairwise preference, calibration, and cost metrics appropriately;
4. diagnose saturation, contamination, Goodhart effects, selection, and judge bias; and
5. build a multi-slice evaluation harness with uncertainty and failure analysis.

## The evaluation record

Every result binds together:

```text
checkpoint and tokenizer
task population and dataset version
prompt template, demonstrations, and tool contract
sampling, context, and inference-time compute
answer parser and grader
aggregation, uncertainty, latency, and cost
```

A zero-shot result, a few-shot result, and a tool-assisted result are not alternative labels for the same number. Model family names are insufficient because public, private, experimental, quantized, and routed variants may behave differently.

## Intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation

Held-out negative log-likelihood or perplexity measures prediction under a specified text distribution. It is dense, cheap, and useful during pretraining. It does not guarantee that knowledge can be elicited through an instruction or that a model behaves safely.

Extrinsic tasks test outcomes: answer a question, solve mathematics, generate code, edit a repository, follow an instruction, or interact with an environment. The task must represent an intended population rather than a collection selected only because it is easy to grade.

## Different benchmark families

[MMLU](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.03300) [@hendrycks2021mmlu] measures multiple-choice performance across academic and professional subjects. [GPQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12022) [@rein2023gpqa] targets difficult graduate-level science questions. [GSM8K](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168) [@cobbe2021gsm8k] and [MATH](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.03874) [@hendrycks2021math] test mathematical problem solving at different levels. [HumanEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374) [@chen2021humaneval] evaluates generated functions with tests, while [SWE-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) [@jimenez2024swebench] evaluates repository-level issue resolution.

These scores cannot be averaged into one natural unit without an explicit aggregation choice. A suite should preserve the individual slices that reveal trade-offs.

## Sampling and pass@$k$

For tasks with executable verification, a model may generate $n$ samples and receive credit if at least one of $k$ selected samples is correct. An unbiased estimator commonly used for pass@$k$ is

$$
\operatorname{pass@}k=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},
$$

where $c$ of $n$ samples pass. The result depends on temperature, sample count, filtering, and the test suite. Pass@1 and pass@100 measure different systems and spend different compute.

## Contamination and saturation

Contamination includes exact questions, solutions, translations, code fixtures, and paraphrases. [LiveBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.19314) [@white2024livebench] uses frequently updated questions and objective grading to reduce some contamination and judge problems. A live benchmark delays contamination; it does not make leakage impossible.

Saturation occurs when strong models cluster near the maximum, leaving too little resolution. Harder replacements can introduce a new problem: a narrow set of extremely difficult questions may no longer represent typical use. Benchmark evolution should preserve the construct being measured rather than chase low scores.

## Preference and model judges

Human pairwise judgments measure which response people prefer under a rubric. Model judges reduce cost but can favor style, verbosity, position, self-similarity, or particular model families. [Chatbot Arena](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v235/chiang24b.html) [@chiang2024chatbotarena] aggregates blinded user preferences, but an Arena rating remains a property of a model identity, traffic distribution, and comparison system.

Judge calibration uses human-labeled audit sets, randomized candidate order, ties, rubric dimensions, and subgroup error analysis. Preference should not be reported as factual correctness.

## Uncertainty and cost

Report confidence intervals or repeated-run variation, especially for small tasks or stochastic inference. Prompt variants and grader sensitivity may contribute more uncertainty than binomial sampling alone.

Capability claims also need a resource axis: input and output tokens, samples, verifier or tool calls, latency, and monetary or energy cost. A reasoning system that improves after sixteen attempts is not directly comparable with a one-attempt baseline.

## Studio: build the harness

Create a versioned evaluation harness containing at least four slices:

1. held-out loss on two data domains;
2. one exact-answer knowledge or reasoning task;
3. one executable code or structured-output task; and
4. one multilingual, preference, or domain-specific slice.

The manifest records all protocol components. Compare exact match, pass@$k$ where appropriate, cost-normalized score, confidence intervals, and a contamination audit. Produce a benchmark card describing intended population, limitations, leakage risks, and failure taxonomy.

## What to remember

1. A result belongs to a checkpoint and complete protocol, not a model name.
2. Perplexity and task outcomes answer different questions.
3. Benchmark families preserve distinct constructs and should remain visible as slices.
4. Pass@$k$ includes a sampling and compute budget.
5. Live data, private tests, and decontamination reduce but do not eliminate leakage.
6. Preference, correctness, calibration, safety, efficiency, and cost need separate measurements.
